kernels.definition: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter that comes in positive and negative forms and determines electric interactions.

definitionAnchor.quote: Electric charge is a conserved property of matter.

facts.text: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

anchor.quote: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

facts.text: Net charge is conserved in an isolated system.

anchor.quote: charge is conserved

kernels.definition: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.

definitionAnchor.quote: The electric field is the electric force per unit charge.

facts.text: The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.

anchor.quote: the direction of the force on a positive test charge

facts.text: Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

anchor.quote: closer field lines indicate a stronger field

kernels.definition: Gauss's law relates the net electric flux through a closed surface to the net charge enclosed by that surface.

definitionAnchor.quote: electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the enclosed electric charge

facts.text: A Gaussian surface is useful for calculating fields when symmetry makes the field magnitude or direction simple on the surface.

anchor.quote: Use symmetry to determine the electric field

facts.text: Zero enclosed charge implies zero net flux, not necessarily zero electric field everywhere on the surface.

anchor.quote: the net flux depends only on the charge enclosed

kernels.definition: Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge; potential difference is the work per unit charge required to move between two points.

definitionAnchor.quote: electric potential energy per unit charge

facts.text: Only potential differences affect work and energy changes in electrostatics.

anchor.quote: only differences in potential energy are physically meaningful

facts.text: Electric field points in the direction of decreasing electric potential.

anchor.quote: electric field points in the direction of decreasing potential

kernels.definition: Capacitance is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference for a conductor or capacitor.

definitionAnchor.quote: capacitance is the amount of charge stored per volt

facts.text: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors.

anchor.quote: energy stored in a capacitor

facts.text: For a parallel-plate capacitor, increasing plate area increases capacitance and increasing separation decreases capacitance.

anchor.quote: capacitance is directly proportional to the area and inversely proportional to the separation

kernels.definition: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes through a surface.

definitionAnchor.quote: electric current is the rate at which charge flows

facts.text: Conventional current direction is the direction positive charge would move.

anchor.quote: direction of positive charge flow

facts.text: Microscopic drift speed is slow even though the electric signal through a circuit propagates rapidly.

anchor.quote: constant velocity, known as the drift velocity

kernels.definition: Electrical resistance describes how strongly a material or device opposes current; Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance for ohmic conductors.

definitionAnchor.quote: The current that flows through most substances is directly proportional to the voltage V applied to it

facts.text: For an ohmic device at fixed temperature, current is proportional to voltage.

anchor.quote: current is proportional to the voltage

facts.text: Resistance depends on material, length, cross-sectional area, and temperature.

anchor.quote: resistance depends on the geometry and material

kernels.definition: A DC circuit is a conducting path with steady current, sources, and components whose voltages and currents obey conservation rules.

facts.text: Series components share the same current; parallel branches share the same voltage.

anchor.quote: series and parallel resistors

facts.text: Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation, and the loop rule expresses energy conservation.

anchor.quote: Kirchhoff's rules

kernels.definition: A magnetic field describes magnetic influence in space and determines magnetic forces on moving charges and currents.

facts.text: Magnetic field lines form closed loops and do not begin or end on isolated magnetic charges.

anchor.quote: magnetic field lines are continuous

facts.text: Currents produce magnetic fields.

anchor.quote: currents produce magnetic fields

kernels.definition: Magnetic force on a moving charge depends on charge, velocity, magnetic field, and the angle between velocity and field.

definitionAnchor.quote: force on a moving charge in a magnetic field

facts.text: The magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.

anchor.quote: perpendicular to the velocity and magnetic field

facts.text: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.

anchor.quote: zero when velocity is parallel to the field

kernels.definition: Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf, with direction constrained by Lenz's law.

definitionAnchor.quote: changing magnetic flux induces an emf

facts.text: Induced current direction opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

anchor.quote: opposes the change in flux

facts.text: Changing field strength, area, or orientation can change magnetic flux.

anchor.quote: magnetic flux

kernels.definition: Inductance measures how a circuit element resists changes in current by inducing emf through changing magnetic flux.

definitionAnchor.quote: self-induced emf opposes the change in current

facts.text: An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field.

anchor.quote: energy stored in the magnetic field

facts.text: A changing current creates a changing magnetic flux that induces back emf.

anchor.quote: Inductance is the property of a device that tells us how effectively it induces an emf in another device

mcItems.q: If two particles possess the same type of electric charge, what is the expected interaction between them?
op: They attract
They repel
They have no interaction
They are conserved
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is 'They repel' because like charges repel. The misconception is choosing 'They attract,' which is incorrect as like charges repel.

mcItems.q: In a closed system, what principle governs the total electric charge?
op: Charge is created
Net charge is conserved
Charge is repulsive
Charge is determined by interaction
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is 'Net charge is conserved' because net charge is conserved in an isolated system. The misconception is choosing 'Charge is created,' which contradicts the conservation principle.

mcItems.q: If a positive test charge is placed in a region where the electric field is directed toward a specific point, what is the resulting motion of that charge?
op: The charge will accelerate in the direction the field points.
The charge will accelerate opposite the direction the field points.
The charge will remain stationary.
The charge will move perpendicular to the field lines.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the first option because the direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate (Claim 1). The most plausible misconception is the second option, which incorrectly suggests the charge accelerates opposite the field direction.

mcItems.ex: The correct choice is the second option because field-line density indicates relative field strength (Claim 2). The most plausible misconception is the first option, which incorrectly suggests an inverse relationship.

mcItems.q: When applying Gauss's law, what relationship connects the net electric flux through a closed surface to the charge within it?
op: The net electric flux is proportional to the net charge enclosed.
The net electric flux is independent of the enclosed charge.
The net electric flux is related to the net charge enclosed by the surface.
The net electric flux is only related to the charge on the surface.
mcItems.ex: Option 2 suggests the flux is independent of the enclosed charge, which contradicts the claim that Gauss's law relates flux to enclosed charge. The correct choice correctly states the relationship described in the source.

mcItems.q: A Gaussian surface is most useful for calculating electric fields when what condition is met?
op: The field magnitude is complex on the surface.
The field direction is highly variable on the surface.
Symmetry makes the field magnitude or direction simple on the surface.
The enclosed charge is non-zero and distributed unevenly.
mcItems.ex: Option 3 describes the condition where symmetry simplifies the field calculation, aligning with the claim. Option 1 and 2 suggest complexity or lack of relationship, which are contrary to the utility of the surface.

mcItems.q: In a parallel-plate capacitor, what happens to the capacitance if the plate area is increased?
op: Capacitance decreases
Capacitance increases
Capacitance remains unchanged
Capacitance is zero
mcItems.ex: Increasing plate area increases capacitance. The misconception is that increasing the area decreases capacitance.

mcItems.q: Where is energy stored in a capacitor?

In the charge on the plates
In the potential difference
In the conductor itself
mcItems.ex: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors. The misconception is that energy is stored in the charge on the plates.

keyTerms.mi: Resistance is solely determined by the material type.
keyTerms.cx: Resistance is determined by material, length, cross-sectional area, and temperature.

keyTerms.df: A mathematical relationship connecting voltage, current, and resistance in circuits involving ohmic conductors.
keyTerms.eg: Calculating the current flowing through a resistor given a known voltage and resistance.
keyTerms.mi: Ohm's law only applies to non-ohmic devices.
keyTerms.cx: Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance for ohmic conductors.

keyTerms.df: A rule expressing charge conservation in a circuit.
keyTerms.eg: Applying Kirchhoff's junction rule to determine the total current entering a node.
keyTerms.mi: Confusing the junction rule with the loop rule, which deals with energy conservation.
keyTerms.cx: The junction rule ensures that the total charge entering a junction equals the total charge leaving it.

keyTerms.df: A rule expressing energy conservation in a circuit.
keyTerms.eg: Using the loop rule to verify that the sum of voltage drops around a closed path equals the net energy change.
keyTerms.mi: Mistaking the loop rule for the junction rule, which governs charge conservation.
keyTerms.cx: The loop rule ensures that the net energy change around any closed path is zero.

mcItems.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between magnetic fields and moving charges?
op: Magnetic fields are determined by the movement of charges.
Magnetic fields determine forces on moving charges.
Moving charges create magnetic fields.
Magnetic fields are static in space.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice states that magnetic fields determine the forces exerted on charges in motion. The misconception is that magnetic fields are created by the movement of charges; the source indicates the reverse relationship (Claim 0).

mcItems.q: What is a characteristic of magnetic field lines?
op: They originate from magnetic charges.
They are open lines that extend to infinity.
They form closed loops.
They only exist around moving currents.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice notes that magnetic field lines form closed loops. The misconception is that field lines are open and extend to infinity; the source specifies they form closed loops (Claim 1).

keyTerms.df: A region of space where magnetic influence is present, dictating forces on moving charges and currents.
keyTerms.eg: The field generated by a straight wire carrying a steady current.
keyTerms.mi: The field is caused by the movement of charges.
keyTerms.cx: The field describes the magnetic influence in space and determines magnetic forces on moving charges and currents.

keyTerms.df: Lines representing the direction of the magnetic influence, which always form closed loops.
keyTerms.eg: The lines surrounding a bar magnet.
keyTerms.mi: Field lines are open and extend indefinitely.
keyTerms.cx: Magnetic field lines form closed loops and do not begin or end on isolated magnetic charges.

mcItems.q: The magnetic force exerted on a moving charge is always oriented in which direction relative to the velocity and the magnetic field?
op: A) Parallel to the velocity and the magnetic field.
B) Perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.
C) In the same direction as the magnetic field.
D) Dependent only on the charge and the field strength.
mcItems.ex: Option B is correct because the magnetic force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field. Option A is incorrect because the force is not parallel to both vectors, and Option C is incorrect because the force is not in the same direction as the field.

keyTerms.df: The interaction between motion and a magnetic field that results in a push or pull on a moving particle.
keyTerms.eg: A current-carrying wire placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences a force perpendicular to the direction of the current.
keyTerms.mi: The force is always parallel to the direction of the current.
keyTerms.cx: The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.

keyTerms.df: A region of space where magnetic effects are present, influencing the motion of charged particles.
keyTerms.eg: The invisible influence surrounding a permanent magnet that affects the path of a nearby moving electron.
keyTerms.mi: The field only exists where there is a moving charge.
keyTerms.cx: The field is a region of space that influences the motion of charged particles.

keyTerms.mi: Believing the current flows in the same direction as the change in magnetic flux.
keyTerms.cx: The induced current direction opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
